chunks.title: Leukocoria
chunks.tldr: Retinoblastoma (mean 18 months, normal-size eye, white mass ± calcification, NVI, seeds). Toxocara (puppies/eating dirt, granuloma, traction; ELISA ≥1:8). Coats (boys, unilateral, telangiectasia + yellow exudative RD = xanthocoria). PFV (small eye, stalk, stretched ciliary processes, cataract). Cataract, astrocytoma (TSC), ROP, FEVR, coloboma, myelinated fibres, Norrie, IP.
points: Measure corneal diameter (small eye = PFV), check iris for NV, lens, dilated fundus.
B-scan (calcification, stalk, RD), FA (Coats/ROP), MRI not CT for RB (radiation → second tumours).
Never do AC tap if RB possible (seeding).
EUA often needed; screen at-risk newborns within 1–2 weeks.
RB Rx: chemoreduction, intra-arterial/intravitreal chemo, cryo, TTT, laser, plaque; enucleation if advanced.
Toxocara: steroids, vitrectomy for traction; albendazole only for systemic.
Coats: FA-guided laser ± anti-VEGF; drain big RD.
PFV: lensectomy + stalk resection; amblyopia therapy (often poor outcome).
chunks.hook: White pupil: RB until proven otherwise — never tap it.

cards.q: Leukocoria in a microphthalmic eye with elongated ciliary processes?
cards.a: Persistent fetal vasculature.

cards.q: Why is MRI preferred to CT for retinoblastoma?
cards.a: Avoids radiation, which increases second malignancy risk (germline RB).

chunks.title: ROP: zones, stages, plus
chunks.tldr: Screen ≤30 weeks or ≤1500 g (or unstable). First exam at 31–32 weeks PMA or 4 weeks after birth, whichever later. Zone I = 2× disc–fovea radius round the disc; II = to nasal ora; III = temporal crescent. Stages: 1 line, 2 ridge, 3 ridge + NV, 4A/4B partial RD (extra/foveal), 5 total. Plus = dilated tortuous posterior vessels in ≥2 quadrants.
points: Risks: prematurity, low weight, oxygen, sepsis, white race, male.
Zone I limit: nasal disc edge at one side of a 28 D lens → temporal field edge.
Don't call zone III until nasal side vascularised to ora.
Aggressive posterior ROP ('rush'): zone I + plus, skips stages, haemorrhages at junction.
Pre-plus = abnormal but not enough for plus.
Dilate with 2 of: phenylephrine 1%, tropicamide 1%, cyclopentolate 0.2–0.5%.
chunks.hook: 1 line, 2 ridge, 3 vessels, 4 partly off, 5 totally off.

cards.q: Criteria for ROP screening?
cards.a: Birth weight ≤1500 g or gestational age ≤30 weeks (plus selected unstable larger infants).

cards.q: Define stage 3 ROP.
cards.a: Ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation.

chunks.title: ROP: treatment & follow-up
chunks.tldr: Type 1 → treat within 48–72 h: zone I any stage + plus; zone I stage 3; zone II stage 2/3 + plus. Type 2 → watch closely: zone I stage 1–2 no plus; zone II stage 3 no plus. Rx: laser to avascular retina (preferred) or intravitreal bevacizumab 0.625 mg (posterior zone I; late recurrence risk). Stage 4–5: vitrectomy.
points: Stop screening: zone III vascularised without prior I/II ROP; PMA 50 weeks without severe ROP; full vascularisation after anti-VEGF.
After anti-VEGF: follow beyond 65–70 weeks PMA (recurrence); consider prophylactic laser if follow-up uncertain.
Lifelong yearly exams: myopia, strabismus, amblyopia, macular drag, cataract, glaucoma, late RD.
Intervals: ≤1 week for zone I or aggressive disease; 2–3 weeks for zone III.

cards.q: Name the three Type 1 ROP criteria.
cards.a: Zone I any stage with plus; zone I stage 3 without plus; zone II stage 2 or 3 with plus.

chunks.title: Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy
chunks.tldr: Looks like ROP in a full-term baby: temporal avascular periphery, fimbriated vessel ends, macular drag, falciform folds, exudate, RD. Bilateral, asymmetric, Wnt pathway (FZD4, LRP5 — osteoporosis, TSPAN12, NDP). Mostly AD. Wide-field FA for patient + family. Laser if NV/exudate; lifelong follow-up.
points: Relatives are often asymptomatic — examine and FA them.
chunks.hook: ROP without prematurity → look at the parents' retinas.

cards.q: FEVR gene linked with early-onset osteoporosis?
cards.a: LRP5.

chunks.title: Esodeviations
chunks.tldr: Pseudoesotropia: wide bridge/epicanthus, normal cover test. Infantile ET (by 6 months, large >40–50 Δ, normal refraction → surgery early). Accommodative (avg 2.5 yrs, hyperopia +3 to +10 → full cycloplegic Rx; high AC/A → bifocals). Acquired non-accommodative — >6 yrs: image for posterior fossa lesion. Sensory ET, divergence insufficiency. Incomitant (worse in side gaze) → VI palsy, restriction → MRI.
points: Correct ≥+2.00 D hyperopia in esotropes; treat amblyopia first.
>6 yrs: push maximum plus without blurring.
High AC/A options: executive bifocals +2.5–3, echothiophate, posterior fixation surgery.
Decompensated accommodative ET when more plus doesn't straighten.
Congenital ET in up to 30% of neuro/developmental disorders — no workup if otherwise normal.
Low vision eye → polycarbonate glasses.

cards.q: Average age of onset of accommodative esotropia?
cards.a: About 2.5 years (6 months–6 years).

cards.q: Acquired comitant esotropia in a 9-year-old — next step?
cards.a: Urgent MRI brain to exclude posterior fossa pathology.

chunks.title: Exodeviations
chunks.tldr: Intermittent XT (commonest in kids, <5 yrs, worse when tired, closes one eye in sun). Control: good (out only after cover), fair (needs blink), poor (spontaneous). Types: basic, true/simulated divergence excess, CI. Rx: glasses, amblyopia, alternate patching/over-minus for fair, surgery for poor control. Congenital XT (rare, CNS association). Sensory, consecutive, Duane type 2.
points: Pseudoexotropia: wide IPD, large positive kappa, temporal macular drag (ROP, FEVR, toxocara).
Convergence paralysis: acute, can't overcome base-out → intracranial lesion.
Review 3–6 monthly.

cards.q: How is control graded in intermittent exotropia?
cards.a: Good (deviates only after cover, recovers quickly), fair (recovers with blink/refixation), poor (deviates spontaneously, stays out).

chunks.title: Strabismus syndromes
chunks.tldr: Duane: retraction + fissure narrowing on adduction; type 1 (poor abduction, eso, face turn toward), type 2 (poor adduction, exo, face turn away), type 3 (both). Brown: can't elevate in adduction (forced ductions +). Monocular elevation deficiency: no elevation anywhere (forced ductions + = IR fibrosis). Möbius: VI + VII. Congenital fibrosis: eyes stuck down, ptosis, chin up.
points: Duane: 85% unilateral; deafness, limb/vertebral anomalies.
Treat for abnormal head posture or primary-position deviation.
Image if acquired, atypical or progressive.
chunks.hook: Duane 1 = can't go out; Duane 2 = can't go in.

cards.q: Face turn in unilateral Duane type 1?
cards.a: Toward the affected side.

chunks.title: Amblyopia: types & signs
chunks.tldr: Reduced best-corrected central vision not explained by pathology, from the first decade. Types: strabismic, anisometropic (≥1.5 D), deprivation (cataract, scar, ptosis, PFV), occlusion (too much patching/atropine — review 1 week per year of age). Signs: crowding, neutral-density filter effect, possible trace RAPD.
points: Can be bilateral (untreated bilateral cataracts).
Lid haemangioma/ptosis can induce astigmatic amblyopia.
Check RAPD with light on-axis (false positives with squint).
chunks.hook: Dim light hurts sick eyes, not lazy eyes (ND filter).

cards.q: What is the neutral-density filter effect?
cards.a: In dim light, VA of an amblyopic eye falls much less than an eye with organic disease.

chunks.title: Amblyopia: treatment
chunks.tldr: Glasses first (full cycloplegic Rx, or cut hyperopia symmetrically). Wait 6–12 weeks of refractive adaptation, then patch the good eye 2–6 h/day (adhesive, on skin) or atropine 1% daily (as good as patching if VA 20/100 or better). Review 1 week per year of age. Stop when equal or no gain after 3 compliant cycles; taper to prevent recurrence.
points: Boost atropine: remove plus lens from the good eye's glasses.
Optical degradation: +9 D lens over the good eye.
Occlusion amblyopia → patch the other eye ~1 day per year of age, re-check.
Delay squint surgery until vision is maximised.
Not reaching 20/40 → polycarbonate protective glasses for sport (one-eyed rule).
Media opacity → remove it first, then patch.
chunks.hook: Specs → wait → patch. Check back 1 week per year.

cards.q: How often to review a 4-year-old on full-time patching?
cards.a: About every 4 weeks (1 week per year of age).

cards.q: Atropine penalisation works as well as patching up to what VA?
cards.a: Mild–moderate amblyopia, 20/100 or better.

chunks.title: Pediatric cataract
chunks.tldr: Mostly idiopathic; familial (AD); galactosaemia (oil droplet, reversible with diet); rubella (pearly nuclear, salt-and-pepper retina — isolate from pregnant women); Lowe (XLR, glaucoma + renal; carrier mums have small opacities); Alport (anterior lenticonus, deafness, nephritis); PFV. Zonular/lamellar = commonest type. ≥3 mm or blunted retinoscopy reflex = visually significant → surgery within days–weeks, then amblyopia therapy.
points: Bilateral → paediatric review for genetic/metabolic cause; unilateral rarely needs systemic workup.
Unilateral + no fundus view → B-scan to exclude posterior PFV.
Tests if indicated: RBC galactokinase/GALT, TORCH titres, urine amino acids.
Anterior polar: small, stable, but can cause anisometropic amblyopia.
Temporising: dilating drops (phenylephrine 2.5%, cyclopentolate 1%) if small central opacity.
Cataract alone doesn't cause RAPD.
chunks.hook: 3 mm and central = it blocks vision. Operate fast, then patch.

cards.q: Most common morphology of congenital cataract?
cards.a: Zonular (lamellar).

cards.q: Anterior lenticonus + haematuria + deafness?
cards.a: Alport syndrome.

chunks.title: Ophthalmia neonatorum
chunks.tldr: Conjunctivitis in the first month. Chemical: hours, gone by 24–36 h. Gonococcus: day 3–4, hyperpurulent, can perforate cornea → admit, ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg IV/IM single dose (max 125 mg) + saline lavage + treat chlamydia too. Chlamydia: 1–2 weeks, mucoid ± pseudomembrane → oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg/d × 14 d (topical alone fails; risk pneumonia/otitis). HSV: IV acyclovir 60 mg/kg/d 14 d (21 if CNS/disseminated).
points: Gram + Giemsa scrapings, blood + chocolate agar (CO₂), chlamydia PCR, viral culture.
Gram stain: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci = gonorrhoea.
Giemsa: basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions = chlamydia; multinucleated giant cells = HSV.
Treat mother and partners for both GC and chlamydia.
Avoid gentamicin prophylaxis (toxic reaction).
Other bacteria: bacitracin (Gram +) or aminoglycoside/FQ (Gram –) ointment × 2 weeks.

cards.q: Why give systemic, not topical, treatment for neonatal chlamydia?
cards.a: Topical alone is ineffective and systemic therapy prevents chlamydial pneumonia/otitis.

cards.q: Hyperpurulent neonatal conjunctivitis on day 3 — drug?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg IV/IM single dose (max 125 mg), admit, also treat chlamydia.

chunks.title: Congenital NLDO
chunks.tldr: Watery eye + sticky lashes, white eye, reflux on sac pressure, starts in first 3 months. Cause: membrane at valve of Hasner. Exclude congenital glaucoma (photophobia, big cloudy cornea). Rx: sac massage q.i.d. ± topical antibiotic; most open by 6–12 months. Probe if still blocked after age 1 (or recurrent infection); then balloon/silicone tubes; DCR last.
points: Dye disappearance test: fluorescein still pooled at 10 min.
Dacryocele: bluish firm mass below medial canthus in first week.
Acute dacryocystitis → systemic antibiotics.
Watch for anisometropic amblyopia.
chunks.hook: Watery + photophobic + big cornea ≠ blocked duct → glaucoma.

cards.q: When is probing indicated for congenital NLDO?
cards.a: Persisting beyond ~1 year, or earlier with recurrent infection/parental request.

chunks.title: Congenital / infantile glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Triad: tearing, photophobia, blepharospasm + cloudy, big eye (cornea >12 mm before age 1), Haab striae (horizontal/curvilinear Descemet breaks), cupping, axial myopia; 80% bilateral. Primary congenital = goniodysgenesis. Commonest paediatric glaucoma overall = after cataract surgery. Rx is surgical: goniotomy (clear cornea) or trabeculotomy; drops only as bridge.
points: DDx: megalocornea (>13 mm, normal IOP), forceps trauma (vertical breaks, unilateral), CHED, PPMD, MPS, NLDO.
EUA: corneal diameter, IOP, pachymetry, gonio, disc, A-scan (17 mm at term → 20 mm at 1 yr).
Halothane/hyperventilation lower IOP; ketamine, succinylcholine, intubation raise it.
Medical: oral acetazolamide 15–30 mg/kg/d (best), topical CAI, timolol 0.25%, PGA.
No brimonidine under age 1 (apnoea, bradycardia); caution <5 yrs or <20 kg.
Amblyopia = commonest cause of vision loss; lifelong follow-up.
Associations: Sturge–Weber, aniridia, Axenfeld–Rieger, Peters, Lowe, rubella, NF1.
chunks.hook: Watery, light-shy baby with big eyes = glaucoma until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Why avoid brimonidine in infants?
cards.a: Crosses blood–brain barrier → apnoea, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia.

cards.q: How do Haab striae differ from forceps injury breaks?
cards.a: Haab: horizontal/curvilinear in an enlarged cornea; forceps: vertical/oblique, unilateral, normal diameter.

chunks.title: Anterior segment dysgenesis
chunks.tldr: Posterior embryotoxon (anterior Schwalbe line; Alagille). Axenfeld–Rieger (iris strands to Schwalbe, corectopia, polycoria; 50–60% glaucoma; PITX2/FOXC1; teeth, umbilical skin). Peters (central corneal opacity + iris/lens adhesion; 'Peters plus' = short stature). Aniridia (PAX6; glaucoma, foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, pannus; sporadic → WAGR, ~30% Wilms → renal US). Microspherophakia (Weill–Marchesani), lenticonus (anterior = Alport), sclerocornea.
points: Aniridia: karyotype/microarray or PAX6 test; renal US at diagnosis then ≥6-monthly to age 7–8 (3-monthly if WT1 deleted).
Ectopia lentis et pupillae: lens and pupil displaced in opposite directions.
Glaucoma meds: β-blocker, PGA, CAI; pilocarpine doesn't work.
Exam every 6 months for life.

cards.q: Genes for Axenfeld–Rieger syndrome?
cards.a: PITX2 and FOXC1 (autosomal dominant).

cards.q: What does WAGR stand for?
cards.a: Wilms tumour, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, Retardation (11p13 deletion).

chunks.title: Congenital ptosis
chunks.tldr: Simple congenital: fibrotic levator → poor levator function, weak crease, lid lag/lagophthalmos in downgaze, chin-up. Blepharophimosis (ptosis, telecanthus, epicanthus inversus; AD). Marcus Gunn jaw-wink (lid rises when chewing). Horner (mild ptosis, miosis, heterochromia if congenital; acquired → think neuroblastoma). Amblyopia mostly from astigmatism.
points: Observe if mild, no amblyopia, no head posture; re-check 3–12 months.
Poor levator function → frontalis sling; moderate/good → levator resection.
Blepharophimosis needs frontalis sling; telecanthus improves with growth.
Jaw-wink often improves by school age; levator resection worsens winking.
Watch exposure keratopathy after surgery.

cards.q: Most common amblyogenic mechanism in congenital ptosis?
cards.a: Induced astigmatism/anisometropia (occlusion less common).

chunks.title: The bilaterally blind infant
chunks.tldr: Roving eyes from 4–8 weeks, poor pupils, no fix/follow by 4 months. Abnormal eye exam: ROP, cataract, aniridia, albinism, optic nerve hypoplasia (double-ring sign; bilateral → MRI for septo-optic dysplasia: GH, cortisol, DI, hypoglycaemic fits), optic atrophy, shaken baby. Normal exam: Leber congenital amaurosis (flat ERG), CSNB (paradoxical pupils), achromatopsia (photophobia, no 30 Hz flicker), cortical visual impairment, delayed visual maturation (normal ERG, improves by 4–12 months).
points: Exam: fix/follow, pupils, nystagmus type, iris transillumination, dilated fundus, cycloplegic refraction.
ERG ± genetics for suspected retinal dystrophy.
MRI if neuro signs, seizures, failure to thrive, ONH, localising nystagmus (seesaw, vertical), or optic atrophy (glioma, craniopharyngioma).
Congenital motor nystagmus: vision usually ≥20/60, null-point face turn.
Counsel parents; low-vision/educational services; genetic counselling.
chunks.hook: Normal-looking eyes + flat ERG = Leber congenital amaurosis.

cards.q: Paradoxical pupil constriction in darkness — two infant causes?
cards.a: Congenital stationary night blindness and achromatopsia (also optic nerve hypoplasia, LCA).

cards.q: Bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia — essential investigation?
cards.a: MRI brain (hypothalamic–pituitary) + endocrine review for septo-optic dysplasia.
